title: EZEKIEL PACKED HIS BELONGINGS AND DUG THROUGH A WALL WHILE EVERYONE WATCHED
paragraphs: EZEKIEL PACKED HIS BELONGINGS AND DUG THROUGH A WALL WHILE EVERYONE WATCHED

They thought they were watching a prophet do something strange. They were actually watching God turn one man's body into a warning—and the most frightening part of Ezekiel 12 may be how easily we can recognize ourselves in the people who watched him.
Imagine opening your door and seeing Ezekiel packing.
Not for vacation.
Not because he had found somewhere better to live.
He was gathering the kind of belongings a person would carry when home was about to become a memory.
People were watching.
That was the point.
Then evening came.
Ezekiel walked toward a wall.
And started digging through it.
With his hands.
No explanation first. No polished sermon. No comfortable religious language to soften what God was saying.
Just a prophet, some belongings, a wall, and the eyes of a rebellious people fixed on him.
And somewhere inside this unsettling scene is a question that refuses to leave us alone:
What if God has been trying to get your attention too... and you have become so accustomed to seeing that you no longer truly see?
Ezekiel 12 begins with words that should make every religious person uncomfortable.
God says of the people:

עֵינַיִם לָהֶם לִרְאוֹת וְלֹא רָאוּ
אָזְנַיִם לָהֶם לִשְׁמֹעַ וְלֹא שָׁמֵעוּ
Einayim lahem lir'ot velo ra'u; oznayim lahem lishmoa velo shame'u.
They had eyes to see, but they did not see; ears to hear, but they did not hear.
The problem was not blindness.
They had eyes.
The problem was not deafness.
They had ears.
Their tragedy was that functioning eyes had stopped perceiving and functioning ears had stopped listening.
God calls them:
בֵּית־הַמֶּרִי — beit-hammeri
A rebellious house.
That is what makes this passage terrifyingly relevant.
Because rebellion does not always scream.
Sometimes rebellion sits quietly in a church.
Sometimes it knows worship songs.
Sometimes it posts Bible verses.
Sometimes it says, “Amen,” while privately protecting the very thing God has been confronting.
Sometimes rebellion looks like hearing the same truth so many times that truth no longer makes you tremble.
You know Jesus died for sinners.
You know repentance matters.
You know bitterness is poisoning you.
You know pornography is not harmless.
You know pride is destroying relationships.
You know the secret messages need to stop.
You know the apology needs to be made.
You know the relationship is pulling you away from Christ.
You know you cannot keep worshiping God publicly while deliberately feeding what He calls sin privately.
You know.
And perhaps that is the frightening part.
Because sometimes our greatest spiritual danger is not ignorance.
It is knowing... and refusing to move.
So God told Ezekiel to make the message impossible to ignore.
עֲשֵׂה לְךָ כְּלֵי גוֹלָה
“Prepare for yourself baggage for exile.”
The Hebrew expression כְּלֵי גוֹלָה — keli golah carries the idea of equipment or belongings associated with exile.
Pack what an exile would pack.
Carry it out.
Do it during the day.
Do it—
לְעֵינֵיהֶם — le'eineihem
“before their eyes.”
That expression keeps returning.
Before their eyes.
Before their eyes.
Before their eyes.
God wanted them watching.
Ezekiel was not performing for applause. He was embodying a warning.
Then came the command that must have looked almost absurd:
לְעֵינֵיהֶם חֲתָר־לְךָ בַקִּיר
“Before their eyes, dig through the wall.”
Picture it.
Dust falling.
Hands working.
People staring.
Perhaps somebody laughed.
Perhaps somebody whispered.
Perhaps someone shook his head at the strange prophet.
But Ezekiel kept digging.
Because obedience sometimes looks foolish to people who cannot yet see what God sees.
Verse 7 is almost painfully simple:
וָאַעַשׂ כֵּן כַּאֲשֶׁר צֻוֵּיתִי
Va'as ken ka'asher tzuvveiti.
“I did so, just as I was commanded.”
There is an entire sermon in that sentence.
God commanded.
Ezekiel obeyed.
He did not need everybody to understand before he obeyed.
He did not need everybody to approve before he obeyed.
He did not rewrite God's command until it became socially comfortable.
He obeyed.
And perhaps somebody reading this already knows exactly where that lands.
There is something God has made clear through His Word that you keep negotiating with.
You keep calling delay “discernment.”
You keep calling compromise “complexity.”
You keep calling bondage “just something I struggle with.”
You keep waiting for obedience to become convenient.
But there are moments when faith sounds remarkably simple:
God spoke.
I obeyed.

That does not mean every strange impulse in our minds is a command from God. Ezekiel was a prophet receiving a specific divine revelation, and Christians must not use this passage to baptize personal impulses with “God told me.”
But where Scripture has already spoken clearly, endless negotiation can become disguised disobedience.
Forgive.
Flee sexual immorality.
Tell the truth.
Love your enemy.
Care for the vulnerable.
Turn from idols.
Confess Christ.
Repent.
Follow Jesus.
Some things do not require another sign.
They require surrender.
And Ezekiel's performance was about something very specific.
This was not originally a motivational metaphor about “breaking through your walls.”
That would flatten the passage.
God Himself explains the sign after verse 7.

Ezekiel was acting out coming judgment and exile. The people of Jerusalem would be driven away, and the ruler in their midst would attempt to leave under darkness. Ezekiel declares, אֲנִי מוֹפֶתְכֶם — ani mofetkhem, essentially, “I am your sign/portent.”
The prophet was carrying tomorrow's catastrophe on his shoulder while people were still living as though tomorrow would never arrive.
And history made the warning horrifyingly concrete.
Jerusalem did fall.
King Zedekiah attempted to flee. He was captured. His sons were killed before him, his eyes were put out, and he was taken to Babylon.
The man who tried to escape under darkness ended up unable to see.
Ezekiel's strange sign had not been religious theater.
God had warned them.
And that is where this ancient scene reaches across the centuries and puts its hand on our shoulder.
Because we are extraordinarily talented at assuming there will always be more time.
More time to repent.
More time to forgive.
More time to come back to church.
More time to take Jesus seriously.
More time to tell our children about Christ.
More time to reconcile with someone.
More time to surrender the addiction.
More time to stop pretending.
More time.
Tomorrow becomes one of the easiest places to hide from God.
But Scripture never gives us tomorrow as property.
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15).
Notice that word.
Today.
The Gospel is not God telling you to clean yourself up enough to deserve Him.
You cannot.
Neither can I.
The Gospel is the announcement that the holy God against whom we have sinned came near to sinners in Jesus Christ.
And this is where Ezekiel's wall eventually forces Christian readers to look beyond Ezekiel.
Not because Ezekiel 12 secretly predicts Jesus digging through a wall—it does not.
But because the judgment against rebellion that Ezekiel announces belongs to the larger biblical story of human sin, divine holiness, judgment, mercy, and ultimately God's saving work in Christ.
Ezekiel carried the belongings of an exile.
Jesus carried a cross.
Ezekiel acted out judgment that guilty people could not indefinitely escape.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God willingly entered suffering for sinners.
“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Christ was not dragged to Calvary because Rome had finally outmaneuvered Him.
He gave Himself.
The hands that could have summoned deliverance were stretched out.
The One without sin stood where sinners deserved to stand.
The righteous for the unrighteous, that He might bring us to God.
And when Jesus cried, “It is finished,” grace did not announce that sin had never mattered.
The cross announced the opposite.
Sin mattered so much that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
Grace is not God pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do to rescue sinners from what their rebellion deserves.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance runs toward grace.
You do not confess because Jesus is reluctant to forgive.
You confess because in Jesus there is forgiveness.
You do not come into the light because you have finally become presentable.
You come because hiding cannot heal you.
Maybe you have spent years carrying something nobody knows about.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your children see the Christian version of you.
Your Facebook friends see the verses.
People see the smile.
But somewhere behind the wall is another room.
And you are exhausted from guarding the entrance.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows what is behind it.
Every compromise.
Every relapse.
Every lie.
Every bitter thought.
Every secret search.
Every night you cried afterward.
Every promise you made to God and broke three days later.
Every moment you wondered whether you had finally gone too far.
He knows.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not, “Hide it better.”
It is:
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation says, “Hide from God because you are filthy.”
The Gospel says, “Run to Christ because He alone can wash sinners clean.”
This is why some walls need to come down.
Not because Ezekiel 12 promises a mystical “breakthrough.”
But because the same human heart capable of watching Ezekiel and refusing to see is alive in every generation.
We build walls between what God says and what we want.
Walls of excuses.
Walls of religious performance.
Walls of “everybody does it.”
Walls of “God understands.”
Yes, God understands more completely than anyone.
Which means He also understands exactly what our sin is doing to us.
The surgeon who loves you does not call the tumor harmless.
And the Savior who died for you loves you far too deeply to rename your chains freedom.
Maybe this article is your moment at the wall.
Not because these words are magical.
Not because Gospel Warrior can save you.
We cannot.
Only Jesus saves.
But perhaps Scripture has exposed something you have been carefully avoiding.
Put the phone down for a moment.
Talk to Jesus.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary required.
Tell Him the truth.
“Lord, I sinned.”
“Lord, I have been hiding.”
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, I am addicted.”
“Lord, I have become cold.”
“Lord, I don't know how to come back.”
“Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.”
And then remember the promise of Scripture: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are words for people who have dirt on them.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Scandalous grace.
Grace strong enough to tell the truth about your sin without abandoning you in it.
Grace that does not merely improve your image.
Grace that begins rewriting your life.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your name has been dragged through conversations you were not in.
Maybe the divorce happened.
Maybe the ministry collapsed.
Maybe the addiction became visible.
Maybe your child discovered what you were hiding.
Maybe you lost years you cannot recover.
Consequences are real, and following Christ does not guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears.
But consequences do not get the final word over the person who belongs to Jesus.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted His people.

The Corinthian church contained people with histories Scripture does not sanitize, yet Paul could write that they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is why our message remains:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Because Jesus is.
Not because sin deserves celebration.
Because redemption deserves proclamation.
Not because your past becomes imaginary.
Because in Christ your past no longer has authority to name your future.
Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this exposed something hidden, do not make the comment section another stage where everybody pretends to be okay.
And believers—when somebody writes those words, do not judge them.
Pray for them.
Let the comments beneath this article become less like an audience and more like people carrying one another toward Jesus.
Then think of one person.
Just one.
The person whose smile has not looked quite right lately.
The friend who stopped attending church.
The believer quietly drifting.
The person carrying shame.
The family member who thinks God could never want them again.
I haven't forgotten you.”
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
If Christ has given you truth, letting someone else encounter that truth can be an act of love.
There may be a night when the feelings return.
When shame starts speaking.
When temptation starts bargaining.
When you need to remember the prophet digging through a wall while everybody watched—and the terrifying danger of seeing without seeing.
Come back.
Read the Scripture again.
Christ alone is our righteousness.
Do it only if you genuinely want to support the mission.
Pray.
Save the article.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.

Because glorifying God is bigger than supporting any particular ministry. But when a ministry faithfully proclaims Christ, those who believe in its mission can glorify God by helping that truth travel farther—through prayer, generosity, encouragement, sharing, and faithful participation.
Somewhere tonight, another person is staring at a wall.
Behind it is the secret.
The shame.
The compromise.
The memory.
The thing they believe has disqualified them forever.
Maybe that person is someone who will see this because you shared it.
Maybe that person...
is you.
Ezekiel dug through a wall because judgment was coming and God's people refused to see.
Centuries later, the Gospel tells us something we dare not refuse to see:
Judgment is real.
Sin is real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is forgiveness.
So is repentance.
So is restoration.
So is Jesus.
The question is no longer whether God has spoken.
The question is whether we will keep watching...
or finally see.
Because the wall you are desperately using to hide your scandal may be the very place where grace is calling you into the light.
